lesson.title: Opposition Without Loss: Understanding Reactance
lesson.summary: Inductors and capacitors oppose current by storing and returning energy rather than dissipating it, and that frequency-dependent opposition is called reactance.
lesson.body:
Resistors oppose current by dissipating energy as heat, and that opposition, resistance, is the same at every frequency, including DC. Inductors and capacitors oppose current differently: they store energy in a magnetic or electric field and hand it back to the circuit a quarter cycle later, so their opposition to current, called reactance, depends on frequency and involves no energy loss at all. Reactance is measured in ohms, just like resistance, but it behaves like an ohm with a 90° twist built in, which is why it eventually needs a sign and the imaginary unit j to describe correctly.

Inductive reactance is XL = ωL, where L is inductance in henries and ω is angular frequency in radians per second; it grows with frequency because a faster-changing current induces a larger opposing voltage in the coil. Capacitive reactance is XC = 1/(ωC), where C is capacitance in farads; it shrinks with frequency because a capacitor charges and discharges more easily when current reverses direction quickly. When an inductor and a capacitor sit in the same series branch, their effects partially cancel, since inductor voltage leads current by 90° while capacitor voltage lags current by 90°, exactly opposite directions; the net reactance is defined as X = XL − XC.

At the standard power frequency of 60 Hz, ω = 2π(60) = 377 rad/s. For an inductor with L = 0.106 H, XL = 377 × 0.106 = 40.0 Ω. For a capacitor with C = 66.3 μF, XC = 1/(377 × 66.3×10⁻⁶) = 1/0.02500 = 40.0 Ω. If this inductor and capacitor were placed in the same series branch, the net reactance would be X = XL − XC = 40 − 40 = 0 Ω: the branch would behave as if it contained no reactance at all at this one frequency, a special condition called resonance, even though each component individually still stores and releases energy every cycle.

The 40 Ω inductive reactance from this example is the same XL used in the series RL circuit, R = 30 Ω, XL = 40 Ω, analyzed in the phasor diagram and phasor addition sections, where it combined with resistance to produce a 50∠53.13° Ω impedance and a current lagging voltage by 53.13°. That combination step, folding resistance and reactance into a single complex number, is the subject of complex impedance, covered next: reactance describes only the frequency-dependent, energy-storing half of a circuit's opposition to current, and it must be paired with resistance to fully describe how a real circuit responds to an AC source.

Both reactance formulas also explain circuit behavior at the extremes of frequency. As frequency approaches zero, the DC limit, XL = ωL approaches zero, so an inductor looks like a short circuit, while XC = 1/(ωC) grows without bound, so a capacitor looks like an open circuit; this matches the everyday fact that a capacitor blocks steady DC current entirely. As frequency grows very large, the opposite happens: an inductor's reactance grows and it begins to block current, while a capacitor's reactance shrinks toward zero and it behaves almost like a short circuit.
